title: Customer interview notes — Quickstart templates onboarding friction (RAG + agents)
content:
Purpose
Collect 4–6 developer interviews focused on onboarding friction for Redwood Hosted API and anticipated quickstart templates (RAG, agents, combined). Capture quotes, current workflow, and prioritized needs to inform template contract + docs.

Method
- 45 min calls (screen-share optional), semi-structured.
- Interviewed engineers with active evaluation or recent PoC.
- Focus areas: time-to-first-success, correctness + reliability defaults, observability, deployment path (local -> staging), safety/security expectations.

TL;DR (top themes)
1) People want a “known-good path” that is production-shaped without turning into a framework.
2) Biggest early failures are not model quality; they’re operational: retries/timeouts/429, streaming disconnects, missing correlation IDs, noisy logs, confusing env vars.
3) RAG ingestion is where time goes to die: chunking defaults, backpressure, and “it works on a small PDF but not real docs.”
4) Observability is a gating requirement for teams beyond hobby use: traceability (request_id/tenant), token/cost attribution, and error taxonomy.
5) Security posture needs to be explicit even in quickstarts: secrets handling, PII guidance, and safe tool calling patterns.

Interview 1 — Devkit AI (PLG-heavy startup; wants <15 min first success)
Date: 2025-12-05
Role: Staff SWE owning LLM platform
Current stack:
- Node + Python mix
- Hosted LLM APIs + self-hosted vector DB in dev
- Uses OpenTelemetry lightly (traces), logs in Datadog
Goals / use case:
- Add RAG to product search + a light “agent” workflow for support triage.
What worked:
- Redwood API integration was “fine once we had the key,” but they had to copy-paste across multiple snippets.
Friction / failure points:
- Env/config confusion: “I never know which env vars are required vs optional until it crashes.”
- 429/backoff confusion: they hit rate limits during load tests and weren’t sure if they should retry, queue, or reduce concurrency.
- Streaming: proxy + web clients caused periodic disconnects; unclear best practice for reconnect/idempotency.
- Lack of defaults for timeouts: “We shipped something that hung in production because we didn’t set a client timeout.”
Quotes:
- “If the quickstart is the first thing I run, it should already have the boring stuff: timeouts, retries, and structured logs.”
- “429s are fine, but tell me what to do. A code sample that’s actually safe is worth more than another doc page.”
Needs (prioritized):
P0
- Single, consistent env var contract across templates/languages (with validation on startup and clear error messages).
- Opinionated retry/backoff strategy with guidance for 429 vs 5xx vs timeouts (and how to set max attempts).
P1
- Streaming reconnect guidance + client patterns for browsers/proxies.
- Minimal dashboards: latency p95, error rate by class, 429 count, and tokens/cost.
P2
- Template should include a “how to extend” section: swap vector DB, swap embedding model, add reranker.

Interview 2 — Aurora Health (regulated-ish; leaning Dedicated/Private later)
Date: 2025-12-08
Role: Senior ML Engineer (platform)
Current stack:
- Python services (FastAPI), Kubernetes
- OTel traces and metrics are mandatory
- Security review is a hard gate
Goals / use case:
- Internal knowledge assistant + ticket triage, eventually needs Private/VPC.
Friction / failure points:
- They can’t adopt samples that ignore data handling: “Every example logs too much by default.”
- Need guidance on deployment modes: “We start on Hosted to learn, but need a clear story for VPC/Private without rewriting everything.”
- Auditability: want consistent request IDs and trace context propagation.
Quotes:
- “If you give me a template, it needs to survive a security review. Otherwise it’s just demo code we can’t use.”
- “We need to see cost per route or per tenant. Without that, we can’t forecast.”
Needs (prioritized):
P0
- PII/logging guidance: what never to log, how to structure logs, and where redaction should happen.
- Trace + log correlation with request_id and tenant_id (even if tenant is just a placeholder header to demonstrate).
P1
- Dedicated/Private readiness notes: network egress, KMS/HSM hooks, audit logs, config separation.
P2
- Example policy for model routing/fallback to maintain uptime.

Interview 3 — Northpeak Bank (strict security + compliance review early)
Date: 2025-12-10
Role: Principal Engineer, security liaison
Current stack:
- Java services + some Python batch; centralized SIEM
- Strong requirements on secrets and dependency scanning
Goals / use case:
- Exploring agent tool calling for internal workflows; sensitive data constraints.
Friction / failure points:
- Tool calling safety is their #1 concern; they want allow-lists and timeouts by default.
- Secrets management: “.env is fine for local, but you must say it’s local-only and how to do it right in prod.”
- Dependency hygiene: examples often pull latest versions or unpinned packages.
Quotes:
- “The fastest way to lose us is a sample that shells out or calls arbitrary URLs with no guardrails.”
- “Tell me exactly what headers you expect and what gets emitted in telemetry. Surprise is the enemy.”
Needs (prioritized):
P0
- Tool allow-list pattern + explicit timeouts + safe error handling (and do not leak tool output into logs by default).
- Clear secrets policy: local dev vs CI vs prod, and rotation notes.
P1
- Dependency pinning and security scanning notes (SCA, secret scanning).
P2
- “Security checklist” section that matches what reviewers look for.

Interview 4 — Helio Support (support automation workload; cares about reliability)
Date: 2025-12-12
Role: Engineering Manager (apps + infra)
Current stack:
- TypeScript/Node backend, Postgres, Redis
- Uses OpenTelemetry for tracing; metrics via Prometheus
Goals / use case:
- Support agent workflow: retrieve relevant KB + draft response, integrate ticketing tool.
Friction / failure points:
- Agent orchestration examples they’ve seen are “too magical” and hard to debug.
- Tool failures are frequent (ticketing API); they want graceful degradation and clear error taxonomy.
- Need a baseline eval harness: “We don’t want to ship regressions every time we tweak prompts.”
Quotes:
- “Don’t hide the steps. Show me a planner/executor or a simple loop, but make it observable.”
- “I care less about perfect prompts and more about: what happens when the tool times out?”
Needs (prioritized):
P0
- Structured errors: distinguish model error vs tool error vs upstream timeout vs 429.
- Built-in circuit-breaker-ish behavior: cap tool concurrency, tool timeouts, retries with jitter.
P1
- Minimal eval hooks (golden prompts) + how to run in CI.
P2
- Reference dashboards/screenshots to align teams on what “healthy” looks like.

Interview 5 — Europay Analytics (EMEA; data residency + cost governance)
Date: 2025-12-16
Role: Staff Data Engineer transitioning to ML apps
Current stack:
- Python, Airflow ingestion, some containerized services
- Data residency constraints; wants clarity on regions and routing
Goals / use case:
- RAG over internal analytics docs; multi-tenant product eventually.
Friction / failure points:
- Ingestion defaults: chunk size and concurrency. Large PDFs cause timeouts and unpredictable performance.
- Cost surprises: “We ran a demo and the token count was 3x what we expected.”
- Confusion on how to tag requests for cost attribution.
Quotes:
- “Give me the knobs, but also give me safe defaults. I don’t know what chunk size should be.”
- “If the console can break down token cost, the template should show me how to attach route/tenant tags.”
Needs (prioritized):
P0
- RAG ingestion guidance: chunking defaults, max doc size behavior, backpressure/queue pattern.
- Cost + token usage instrumentation examples (per request, per route).
P1
- Region/data residency callouts: what to configure, what to verify.
P2
- A “resource sizing” cheat sheet for local Docker and small k8s.

Cross-interview patterns (what to bake into templates)
P0 (must-have for v1)
- Config contract + validation:
  - One set of env vars across languages (names + semantics) and a startup validator that prints actionable errors.
  - Example: REDWOOD_API_KEY, REDWOOD_BASE_URL, REDWOOD_MODEL, REDWOOD_TIMEOUT_MS, REDWOOD_MAX_RETRIES, REDWOOD_TENANT_ID (optional), REDWOOD_ROUTE (optional), OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT.
- Reliability defaults:
  - Timeouts enabled by default.
  - Retry/backoff guidance by error type (esp. 429).
  - Graceful shutdown and request cancellation.
- Observability:
  - request_id correlation (generate if missing, echo if provided) and trace context propagation.
  - Standard log fields (request_id, tenant, model, route, error_class).
  - Minimal metrics to power default dashboard panels (latency p50/p95, error rate, 429s, timeouts, tokens in/out).
- Security posture:
  - Secrets handling guidance (local vs prod) + “don’t commit .env” and secret scanning.
  - Tool calling guardrails (allow-list, timeouts, output schema validation).
  - PII logging guidance (what not to log; redaction note).

P1 (strong should-have)
- RAG ingestion realism:
  - A default ingestion worker with concurrency controls.
  - Sensible chunking defaults + clear tuning guide.
  - “Works on a folder of PDFs” story with guardrails (max file size, supported formats).
- Deployability:
  - Docker Compose path that mirrors production shape.
  - Minimal k8s manifests + notes for Dedicated/Private.
- Eval hooks:
  - Minimal prompt set + a regression runner example.

P2 (nice-to-have)
- Vector DB adapter interface (show how to swap) without boiling the ocean.
- Reference screenshots and “what good looks like” panel guide.

Open questions / follow-ups
- Confirm final env var names with SDK + docs teams (avoid drift between Python and TS templates).
- Decide what we consider a “tenant_id” in examples (header vs config) to avoid implying multi-tenant security guarantees.
- Clarify recommended patterns for streaming reconnect and idempotency keys (esp. behind proxies).
- Determine what we can safely log by default while still being useful for debugging.

Proposed next steps
1) Convert P0 needs into the template contract checklist and CI validation (ENG-2845).
2) Add a “Common failure modes” section in each template README (429s, streaming disconnects, timeouts, region/model mismatch).
3) Build an “observability pack” that matches the contract and includes a short panel guide (ENG-2846).
4) Security review of tool calling patterns and secrets guidance; incorporate explicit do/don’t bullets (ENG-2849).

Appendix: raw JTBD statements (verbatim)
- “When I paste the code and run it, I want to know it’s not going to hang forever and I want logs that I can grep.”
- “When rate limits happen, I want the app to degrade gracefully instead of thundering herding.”
- “When the tool fails, I want the LLM to recover without leaking sensitive tool output.”
- “When I run a RAG demo with real docs, I want ingestion not to fall over and I want to understand cost.”

Notes
- Several interviewees asked for a single landing page that helps them choose between RAG vs agents vs combined, with expected setup time and prerequisites.
- Two teams explicitly said they will not adopt templates without OTel traces and structured logs out of the box.
